records.sourceFile: Nutritional interventions to support acute mTBI recovery.pdf

paper.citation: Finnegan E, Daly E, Pearce AJ, Ryan L. Nutritional interventions to support acute mTBI recovery. Front Nutr. 2022;9:977728.
paper.abstract: The authors systematically review human nutritional interventions given within 14 days of mild traumatic brain injury. They conclude that certain therapies, especially omega-3 fatty acids, show potential, but that heterogeneous, small studies do not allow definitive recommendations.
paper.tldr: Nutrition for acute concussion has promising but weak evidence, with the strongest signal for omega-3 DHA in small trials. Most included studies are not in athletes, so the findings cannot yet set a concussion nutrition protocol.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021226819). Five databases were searched to 6 January 2021 for human studies of nutrition or nutritional interventions in mild TBI within 14 days of injury, with screening of titles, abstracts and full texts, and quality rating against the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics checklist. Eleven studies were included and were synthesised qualitatively because data were insufficient for meta-analysis.
paper.findings: In a sports concussion trial of 40 adolescents, DHA (2,000 mg) for 12 weeks gave symptom resolution in 16.1 days versus 20.9 days for placebo (p=0.082, not significant). In an NCAA trial of 55 student athletes, 2,200 mg DHA for 30 days gave return to play in 9.1 days versus 10.7 days for placebo (p=0.397, not significant). In 81 military personnel with blast-related mTBI, N-acetyl cysteine (early and delayed groups combined) gave higher day-7 symptom resolution than placebo (OR 3.6, p=0.006), and in 17 adolescents magnesium oxide reduced post-concussion symptom scores at 48 hours (p=0.016) with 50% loss to follow-up. A 5-day cerebrolysin infusion improved CASI scores from baseline within the treated group in a 32-person pilot, with no significant between-group MMSE difference (p=0.111), and the citicoline phase III trial (n=1,213) found no benefit over placebo at day 90.
paper.limitations: Included trials are small, use different doses, timings and outcomes, and the three omega-3 trials are abstracts with incomplete data. In the NCAA trial, 7 of 62 athletes (6 DHA, 1 placebo) who did not return to play within 30 days were excluded from the analysis. The abstract's claim that patients who met calorie and protein needs within 96 h had a reduced hospital length of stay is not supported by the reported data: the only nutrition-intake study was observational, found intakes below requirement, and did not compare length of stay; the discussion presents reduced length of stay only as a possible benefit. The 'positive' labels are quality ratings, and the count of nine positive outcome studies is not consistent with the cited studies' results.
paper.practicalImplications: The one observational study found hospitalised TBI patients ate about 23% of estimated calorie needs and 15% of protein needs on day 1, so monitoring early food intake in admitted patients is reasonable. Do not start omega-3, N-acetyl cysteine or magnesium as standard post-concussion care on the basis of this review; the athlete trials did not show statistically significant benefit. The vitamin D evidence comes from one retrospective study of mostly mild to moderate TBI with benefits at 12 weeks, not in the acute phase.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not assess athletic performance or training outcomes. Its only sport-specific trials are small and did not show statistically significant differences in return to play.
paper.rtp: The review cannot be used to shorten concussion management or to set a return-to-play timeline. The authors state that no nutritional recommendations exist for post-mTBI recovery, and the two athlete trials did not show statistically significant return-to-play differences.

records.sourceFile: Observation of risk for concussion following 'lowering the helmet to initiate contact' penalities in the NFL.pdf

paper.citation: Waller G, Domingue GA, Kintada JR, Box MW, Steinmetz G, Rowles D. Observation of risk for concussion following 'lowering the helmet to initiate contact' penalties in the NFL. Journal of Orthopaedic Reports. 2024;3:100347.
paper.abstract: Observational study of NFL players diagnosed with concussion from 2015 to 2022 and of 'lowering the helmet to initiate contact' penalties from 2018 to 2020, using publicly reported league injury and play data. The authors compared penalty-linked concussions with the overall per-play concussion rate and tested trends across years.
paper.tldr: Three of 86 'lowering the helmet' penalties in 2018 to 2020 were followed by a concussion (3.5%), above the league's 0.45% per-play rate, although the two rates use different denominators. The overall NFL concussion rate fell over 2015 to 2022, but the study cannot show the penalty caused that fall.
paper.methods: Retrospective descriptive study using NFL.com injury reports, penalty records and team play counts for 2015 to 2022. Online game recordings and play tracking were used to identify the player hit on each penalized play, and a second researcher verified the records. Friedman tests compared years, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction compared pairs of years, and linear regression and Pearson correlation assessed trends.
paper.findings: Mean regular-season concussion incidence was 0.45% of plays (SD 0.08%). Three of 86 penalties (3.5%) from 2018 to 2020 were followed by a concussion; in each case a defensive player was penalized and the concussed player was an offensive player. The Friedman test showed differences across years (chi-square = 16.0, p = 0.0003), but no pairwise year-to-year difference was significant after Bonferroni correction. The concussion rate per play showed a significant negative linear trend from 2015 to 2022 (R² = 0.575, p = 0.029).
paper.limitations: Only three concussions followed penalties, and the paper is inconsistent on details: the discussion refers to four concussions on these plays, and the penalty is said to have been grouped under unnecessary roughness in 2020 and in 2021. The 3.5% rate is per penalty and the 0.45% rate is per play, and no statistical test compares them, so the paper's conclusion that penalized plays carry a higher incidence is a descriptive comparison of unlike rates. Data were collected retrospectively from public NFL reports, equipment, practice, reporting and protocol changes could explain the trend, and the authors note possible underreporting of concussions.
paper.practicalImplications: Because athletes underreport concussions, the authors advise thorough medical evaluation after head-first contact whether or not a foul is called. They also suggest teaching players to avoid lowering-the-helmet positions, a recommendation that rests on three events. The data cannot show whether the penalty itself reduces concussions, so staff should not assume it does.
paper.athleteDev: The authors recommend coaching tackling and contact positions that do not lead with the helmet, but the supporting data are three concussions in 86 penalties. Track head-first contact in your own data, and do not use the 3.5% figure as a per-play risk benchmark.
paper.rtp: The study covers concussion occurrence and penalty records and does not assess recovery time, symptom management or return-to-play criteria. It cannot be used to make return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Optimizing concussion care seeking - The influence of previous concussion diagnosis status on baseline assessment outcomes.pdf

paper.citation: Lynall RC, D'Lauro C, Kerr ZY, Knight K, Kroshus E, Leeds DD, et al. Optimizing Concussion Care Seeking: The Influence of Previous Concussion Diagnosis Status on Baseline Assessment Outcomes. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional analysis of 29,934 college athletes and military cadets in the CARE Consortium at preseason baseline. Participants reporting at least one undiagnosed concussion (5.3%) had higher symptom severity and BSI-18 scores and mixed neurocognitive results, with no differences in mental status or balance, compared with those with no concussion history or only diagnosed concussions.
paper.tldr: In nearly 30,000 college athletes and cadets, those reporting at least one undiagnosed concussion had more symptoms and psychological distress at baseline, along with mixed neurocognitive results. Mental status and balance were unchanged, and the design cannot show whether the undiagnosed injuries caused these differences.
paper.methods: Participants completed a baseline questionnaire on concussion history and diagnosis status, followed by the SCAT3 symptom checklist, BSI-18, SAC, BESS and one of four computerized neurocognitive tests depending on site (ImPACT, CNS Vital Signs, ANAM or CCAT). Three history groups were compared using multiple linear regression for continuous outcomes and negative binomial models for symptom and BSI-18 scores, adjusted for sex, race, ethnicity, sport contact level, concussion count and clustering by site. Differences counted as meaningful only if the 95% CI excluded the null and the effect was at least small (effect size 0.20 or IRR 1.10).
paper.findings: Compared with no concussion history, at least one undiagnosed concussion was associated with higher SCAT symptom severity (IRR 1.39, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.61) and BSI-18 scores (IRR 1.31, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.48), with similar IRRs against the all-diagnosed group (1.38 and 1.39). The authors report worse performance for the undiagnosed group on 6 neurocognitive comparisons (CNS Vital Signs visual memory, processing speed and reaction time; ANAM simple reaction time test 1 and procedural reaction time) and better performance on 2 (ANAM matching to sample, CCAT learning). Participants with only diagnosed concussions did not differ from those with no history on symptoms or BSI-18, and no group differences were found on the SAC or BESS.
paper.limitations: Concussion history and diagnosis status were self-reported, diagnosis categories were collapsed, and medical records were not reviewed, so some injuries may be missed or misclassified; the authors also note that a more thorough history reporter may report symptoms more thoroughly at baseline. The cross-sectional design cannot show causation, and neurocognitive results were inconsistent across platforms, each tested at only 1 to 25 sites (CNS Vital Signs n=1087, ANAM n=875, CCAT n=1407). The Results list ANAM simple and procedural reaction time as worse in the undiagnosed group, but the Discussion calls them faster; the abstract gives a symptom IRR of 1.38 where Table 3 gives 1.39 against no history; and minus signs in the extracted Table 3 mean differences are garbled, so only the text and IRRs are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest previous concussion diagnosis status is another factor that may affect baseline performance, so recording whether past concussions were diagnosed can help when interpreting baseline symptom and BSI-18 scores. Their main recommendation is interventions that increase timely concussion diagnosis.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured baseline symptoms and neurocognitive scores, not athletic performance, and the differences were modest. A history of undiagnosed concussion may be worth noting when a baseline is used as a reference, but the study does not support performance decisions.
paper.rtp: The study does not measure recovery or return-to-play timing, so it cannot show that undiagnosed concussions slow recovery or change when an athlete can return. Its relevance to return to play is indirect: a history of undiagnosed concussion may mean that baseline symptom or cognitive scores differ, which can affect how post-injury scores are read.

records.sourceFile: Outcome of turf toe injuries in NFL players.pdf

paper.citation: Madi NS, Parekh TJ, Parekh SG. Outcome of Turf Toe Injuries in NFL Players. The Journal of Foot & Ankle Surgery. 2022.
paper.abstract: Retrospective study of 67 NFL players with 71 turf toe injuries during the 2011 to 2014 seasons. Among 16 offensive skill players, power ratings did not differ significantly before versus after injury, or compared with uninjured running backs and wide receivers.
paper.tldr: In NFL players with turf toe injuries, a yards-and-touchdowns power rating did not change significantly after injury, either compared with before injury or with uninjured running backs and wide receivers. The performance group was small (16 players), and the study does not show whether injury grade matters.
paper.methods: Turf toe injuries from the 2011 to 2014 seasons were identified from online NFL injury reports, player registries and news sources. For offensive skill players with at least 200 total power-rating points over six seasons, the power rating (total yards divided by 10 plus touchdowns times 6) was calculated for three seasons before injury, the index season and two seasons after, and compared with 149 uninjured running backs and wide receivers from 2012 using two-sided t tests.
paper.findings: Sixty-seven players had 71 turf toe injuries; 9 (13%) were placed on injured reserve, 8 (12%) had operative repair, and the average time missed was 3.2 games. Among the 16 offensive skill players, power rating was 105.7 per season before injury, 87.3 in the index season and 115.5 afterward (P=.53), and 7.3, 6.9 and 8.1 per game (P=.4). Post-injury values did not differ from controls (115.5 vs 99.2 per season, P=.24; 8.1 vs 7.2 per game, P=.27).
paper.limitations: Data came from public online sources without clinical records, and injury grade and playing surface were not analysed in the performance comparison. The performance cohort was only 16 players and required at least 200 power-rating points over six seasons, which favours players who returned and produced (inference); the authors acknowledge a few productive post-injury seasons could skew results. The Discussion describes 'improvements in play' and a return to preinjury level, but the differences were not significant (P=.53 and P=.4), so they show no detectable change rather than gains.
paper.practicalImplications: For NFL running backs and wide receivers with turf toe, staff can note that power ratings were not significantly lower after injury in this small sample, but should not extend that to other positions. Injury grade was not analysed, and 8 of the 67 players in the cohort had operative repair.
paper.athleteDev: The study tracks a yards-and-touchdowns power rating for running backs and wide receivers, and found no significant change after turf toe injury in 16 offensive skill players. It does not measure speed, cutting or push-off power, so it should not be used to judge performance in other positions or sports.
paper.rtp: The study shows only that 16 productive offensive skill players had similar power ratings after injury; one of them was placed on injured reserve and did not return the next season. It does not give return-to-play rates or timelines by injury grade or treatment, and the authors state that grade-specific studies are needed.

records.sourceFile: Overlapping mechanisms of exterional heat stroke and malignant hyperthermia - Evidence vs conjecture.pdf

paper.citation: Laitano O, Murray KO, Leon LR. Overlapping mechanisms of exertional heat stroke and malignant hyperthermia: evidence vs. conjecture. Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: This review compares exertional heat stroke (EHS) and malignant hyperthermia (MH) in pathophysiology, incidence, diagnosis and treatment. The authors find that the two conditions share clinical features, but the evidence that they share a calcium-dysregulation mechanism is limited. They conclude that dantrolene's effect in EHS is uncertain, while rapid cooling remains the most effective EHS treatment.
paper.tldr: Exertional heat stroke and malignant hyperthermia look alike, but the review finds no robust evidence that they share a mechanism. Rapid cooling remains the treatment for heat stroke, and dantrolene's benefit in EHS is unproven.
paper.methods: Narrative review that draws on case reports of awake MH (Table 1), the EMHG and NAMHG in vitro contracture test protocols (Table 2), and a small number of EHS incidence and cohort reports. The paper describes no systematic literature search.
paper.findings: Awake MH during exercise or heat exposure shares symptoms with EHS, but EHS patients usually show muscle flaccidity on collapse while MH causes rigidity. In a triathlon series, 12 of 68,557 starters (1.74 per 10,000) were diagnosed with EHS. In a French military cohort of prior EHS cases, 45.6% tested positive on IVCT, but the authors note the test has never been validated for EHS. Dantrolene tested in EHS has shown either a lack of clinical efficacy or mixed results, while rapid cooling is described as the most effective EHS treatment.
paper.limitations: The paper is a narrative review with no described search method, so evidence selection cannot be checked. Table 1 gives 466 EHS patients for the French cohort while the text gives 454. The authors note that IVCT results have low specificity (Table 2 lists 78% for NAMHG and 93.6% for EMHG). Much of the evidence is from case reports.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should treat an athlete who collapses with hyperthermia as an emergency and start rapid cooling, which the authors identify as the most effective EHS treatment. Staff should not assume dantrolene helps EHS, since the authors describe the evidence as mixed and note possible side effects. Rigidity, a core temperature that keeps rising after exercise stops, and family history are features the review links to awake MH, so these should prompt medical review.
paper.athleteDev: Exertion in hot, humid conditions can trigger both EHS and awake MH, so performance staff can use the awake-MH risk factors the review lists (family history of MH, pre-existing muscle conditions, large muscular build, recent or concurrent illness, prior psychological or environmental stress) to flag athletes for medical attention during hot training. The review does not validate any screening tool for these factors.
paper.rtp: The review does not give return-to-play criteria. It cannot be used to decide whether an athlete with a prior EHS or MH episode can return to hot-weather training, since the authors describe this as a matter still under debate.

records.sourceFile: Overview of treatment options for mild traumatic brain injury - A literature review.pdf

paper.citation: Patel H, Polam S, Joseph R. Overview of treatment options for mild traumatic brain injury: a literature review. Cureus. 2024;16(4):e59021.
paper.abstract: This literature review summarizes concussion diagnosis and treatment options for athletes, including rest, a jugular vein compression collar, osteopathic manipulative medicine, herbal and pharmacological treatments, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, blood-flow-restricted interval training, aerobic exercise and vestibular rehabilitation. It also reviews the Amsterdam 2022 consensus statement. The authors state that there is no definitive treatment for concussion and that the evidence for most options is limited.
paper.tldr: There is no definitive concussion treatment, and care relies on brief relative rest followed by a stepwise return to activity with medical clearance before contact. The best athlete-specific evidence summarized is one adolescent trial of early aerobic exercise; the other options rest on small, pilot or non-athlete studies.
paper.methods: Literature review of PubMed, Embase and Medline for April 2012 to April 2022, limited to peer-reviewed English-language human studies of athletes with diagnosed concussion and treatment approaches. The search returned 163 articles, and 24 were included. The Amsterdam 2022 consensus statement was added to cover recent developments. No quality appraisal method is described.
paper.findings: In one trial of adolescents with sport-related concussion, aerobic exercise started within 10 days was reported to improve symptoms within four weeks and to lower the risk of long-term symptoms by 48%. In a trial of patients after traumatic brain injury, group vestibular rehabilitation improved dizziness and mobility, but control and treatment groups reached the same level by the second follow-up; the review also states, citing that trial, that starting within 30 days leads to earlier return to play. Hyperbaric oxygen in persistent post-concussion syndrome, methylphenidate or galantamine in PTSD and/or TBI patients, the herbal product MLC901 in a pilot TBI trial, and blood-flow-restricted interval training in a pilot study were each reported to improve symptoms, and one cited study found people who did not rest after concussion recovered faster than those who rested.
paper.limitations: The paper gives only a brief search description and no quality appraisal, so selection cannot be checked. Several trials cited are in traumatic brain injury, PTSD or post-concussion patients rather than athletes, and the interval training (ref 20) and MLC901 (ref 9) studies are pilot studies, yet Table 1 says interval training 'can be used to aid athletes in recovery'. Table 1 and the Discussion say galantamine can be used with methylphenidate, but the body text and reference title describe the McAllister trial as testing methylphenidate or galantamine, and the conclusion mentions optometry, which the body text does not discuss.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should follow a stepwise return-to-activity progression after 24 to 48 hours of relative rest, with at least 24 hours between steps and medical clearance before full-contact practice. Athletes with signs such as loss of consciousness, seizures, ataxia, confusion or amnesia should be removed from play immediately and returned only after medical clearance. The review, summarizing the Amsterdam statement, says dizziness, neck pain or headache beyond 10 days warrants cervicovestibular rehabilitation; the hyperbaric, herbal, drug and blood-flow-restriction options should not be treated as established athlete treatments on this evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Graded aerobic work is part of the review's recovery approach, so performance staff can plan conditioning during a concussion only under the direction of the medical team. The review warns that weightlifting or sprinting can raise heart rate rapidly, which is not advised when symptoms are being assessed.
paper.rtp: The review describes a stepwise progression (rest, light aerobic, sport-specific, non-contact, full-contact practice, then return) with at least 24 hours between steps, and says the process applies regardless of age or level of sport. It also says the steps should allow at least one week and that timing depends on age, sport and history, so it gives no fixed return-to-play timeline.

paper.citation: Hazzard S, Bacevich B, Lustig M, Lonati D, Asnis P. Preferences Including Graft Choice, Lateral Augmentation, and Rehabilitation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Among National Football League Team Orthopaedic Surgeons. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2025;7(4):101161.
paper.abstract: A multiple-choice survey was sent to NFL team physicians who perform sports medicine knee surgery, and 51 of 97 (53%) responded. Patellar tendon autograft was the favored graft for the three hypothetical athletes, with quadriceps tendon second. Most respondents would not recommend primary ACL repair, outpatient physical therapy beyond team staff, or a brace for return to play.
paper.tldr: Among 51 NFL team knee surgeons who responded to a survey, patellar tendon autograft was the most common graft choice in three hypothetical ACL reconstruction scenarios, with quadriceps tendon second. These are stated surgeon preferences, not outcome data, and do not show that one graft performs better.
paper.methods: An 11-question online survey was emailed four times in May 2023 to 97 NFL team physicians identified through public web searches as performing sports medicine knee surgery, with NCAA physicians excluded. The survey was designed to resemble a 2014 NFL and NCAA survey and asked about graft choice for three hypothetical athletes, primary repair, femoral tunnel drilling, lateral augmentation, return-to-sport criteria and bracing. Responses were summarized by question with no advanced statistical analysis.
paper.findings: Of 51 respondents, the mean experience with ACL surgery was 19.6 years (SD 11.4) and the mean number of ACL reconstructions in 2022 was 103.9 (SD 46.6). Patellar tendon autograft was chosen by 48 (94%) surgeons for the 20-year-old running back, by 33 (65%) for the 25-year-old recreational athlete and by 20 (39%) for the 35-year-old. Two surgeons (4%) would choose primary repair for the running back, 43 (84%) would add lateral augmentation only if certain findings were present, 38 (76%) did not recommend a brace and 38 (75%) recommended team staff rehabilitation alone. Compared with the 2014 survey, the authors report hamstring autograft preference fell from 42.3% to 8% for the 25-year-old, and transtibial femoral drilling fell from 25% to 14%, while anteromedial portal drilling was 71% and retrograde drilling 16%.
paper.limitations: The survey was not validated, had no advanced statistical analysis and reached 53% of identified surgeons, so responder bias is possible. NCAA physicians were excluded, which limits direct comparison with the 2014 survey, and the text dates the survey to May 2023 while the results label it 2024. The abstract gives 96% for lateral augmentation, but the results report 43 (84%) and the discussion '>80%', so this record uses the results figure; the brace question also totals 50 answers (12 yes, 38 no), so 76% is of 50 rather than 51 respondents.
paper.practicalImplications: The results describe how NFL team knee surgeons approach ACL graft choice and rehabilitation, including that patellar tendon autograft is the most common choice and that bracing is not routinely recommended. Because the findings are hypothetical preferences, they should not be applied as a protocol for an individual athlete, and decisions should rest on the injury, the surgeon's assessment and local rehabilitation practice.
paper.athleteDev: The study reports surgeon preferences for ACL reconstruction, not athlete performance. It cannot show how graft choice or lateral augmentation affects speed, strength or other performance measures.
paper.rtp: The study can be used only to describe surgeon return-to-sport criteria. Fifteen surgeons (29%) required passing strength and agility tests, 13 (25%) also required at least 9 months after surgery, and 38 (76%) did not recommend a brace. It cannot show which return criteria reduce reinjury, so it should not be used as evidence for return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Past-season, pre-season and in-season risk assessment of groin problems in male football players - A prospective full-season study.pdf

paper.citation: Esteve E, Casals M, Saez M, Rathleff MS, Clausen MB, Vicens-Bordas J, et al. Past-season, pre-season and in-season risk assessment of groin problems in male football players: a prospective full-season study. Br J Sports Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: A prospective full-season cohort of 245 male amateur football players examined past-season groin pain, pre-season adductor squeeze strength, age and in-season HAGOS (Sport) scores as risk factors for in-season groin problems. Past-season groin pain and lower pre-season long-lever adductor squeeze strength were associated with higher risk, while short-lever strength, age and HAGOS (Sport) were not associated in the main models.
paper.tldr: Players with groin pain in the previous season had about 2.4 times the risk of a groin problem in the new in-season. Higher pre-season long-lever adductor squeeze strength was linked to lower risk, but this comes from one cohort of amateur players.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort of 245 amateur male players from 17 teams (tiers IV to VI), followed for a 39-week competitive in-season. Pre-season measures were past-season groin pain (yes/no), age, and short- and long-lever adductor squeeze strength normalised to body mass and lever length. In-season groin problems were recorded as time-loss injuries or as self-reported groin pain without time loss, with HAGOS (Sport) every 4 weeks. Two-part Bayesian logistic models (INLA) estimated relative risks adjusted for football exposure, with team and player random effects.
paper.findings: Of 245 players, 99 (40.4%) had a groin problem, covering 233 in-season problems (35 with time loss, 198 without). In the long-lever model, past-season groin pain was associated with higher risk (RR 2.40, 95% credibility interval 1.52 to 3.74), and each 1 N·m/kg increase in long-lever squeeze strength with lower risk (RR 0.65, 0.42 to 0.99); short-lever strength (RR 0.72, 0.39 to 1.30), HAGOS (Sport) and age (RR 1.05, 0.99 to 1.11) were not associated. In the split analysis, past-season pain was associated with problems without time loss (RR 2.60, 1.63 to 4.20) but not with time-loss problems (RR 1.55, 0.72 to 3.29), and long-lever strength was associated with time-loss problems (RR 0.50, 0.26 to 0.94) but its interval crossed 1 for problems without time loss (RR 0.67, 0.43 to 1.04).
paper.limitations: Convenience sample of amateur players, 69 players (28.2%) dropped out, and exposure was estimated for two teams with incomplete records. The abstract's 'Players (n=245) suffering from groin pain during the past-season' can be read as 245 players with past-season pain, but Table 1 shows 245 is the whole sample and 77 (31.4%) reported past-season pain; the results text also gives the past-season interval as 1.52 to 3.54 while Table 2 gives 1.52 to 3.74. The abstract says age was not associated, yet Table 3 shows a borderline age association for problems without time loss (RR 1.05, 1.00 to 1.11).
paper.practicalImplications: Pre-season screening should record past-season groin pain whether or not it caused time loss, since it was the clearest risk marker here. Long-lever adductor squeeze strength is a reasonable pre-season baseline for flagging players for closer in-season monitoring. The study did not test whether training to raise strength reduces groin problems.
paper.athleteDev: Pre-season long-lever adductor strength can serve as a baseline measure within individual planning for amateur players. The study did not measure performance outcomes, so it does not show that changing strength improves performance.
paper.rtp: Limited. The study models the risk of new in-season groin problems, not recovery or return to play after an injury, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Pectoralis Major Injuries in the   National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Sahota S, Gibbs DB, Lawton CD, Balderama ES, Chambers CC, Mack CD, et al. Pectoralis major injuries in the National Football League. Sports Health. 2019.
paper.abstract: A retrospective review of NFL Injury Surveillance System data over 15 seasons identified 211 pectoralis major injuries, 132 strains and 79 ruptures. Ruptures treated operatively missed significantly more days than ruptures treated without surgery or with unknown treatment.
paper.tldr: Pectoralis major injuries are uncommon in the NFL, and most occur in games. Ruptures repaired surgically kept players out for about 147 days on average versus about 77 days for the no-surgery or unknown group, which helps frame expected time loss.
paper.methods: Retrospective review of primary pectoralis major strains (grades 1 and 2) and ruptures (grade 3) in the NFL Injury Surveillance System, 2000 to 2014, excluding offseason and conditioning injuries, with game injuries used for position, activity and contact-type analyses. Incidence was expressed per 10,000 athlete-exposures, calculated by assuming 53 players per team and 105 practices per year rather than counting actual participation. Rates were compared with exact Poisson tests and days missed with t tests.
paper.findings: Of 211 injuries, 132 were strains and 79 were ruptures. Strain incidence was 0.41 and rupture incidence 0.25 per 10,000 athlete-exposures, and game rates were far higher than practice rates (strains 1.91 versus 0.12; ruptures 1.33 versus 0.03). Of 69 ruptures with treatment data, 52 (75.4%) were treated surgically and missed 146.7 ± 55.0 days versus 77.2 ± 72.9 days for no surgery or unknown treatment (P < 0.01); among 130 strains, the 10 treated surgically missed 151.2 ± 62.9 days versus 18.1 ± 28.7 days (P < 0.01). Defensive players had more in-game injuries than offensive or special teams players for both types.
paper.limitations: Retrospective surveillance data depend on club reporting, and the 2014 move to the clinical EMR changed how injuries were captured. Exposure denominators were assumed (53 players per team in every practice and game), which the authors note overstates exposure because fewer players are actually exposed, so incidence rates are estimates and likely understated. Days missed can be underestimated because injuries without a return date by the June 2015 data cutoff were excluded, the 'no surgery' groups include unknown treatment, the surgical strain group is small (10 cases), and no performance or functional outcomes were available.
paper.practicalImplications: Players with a rupture that needs operative repair should be counselled to expect a substantially longer absence, around 5 months on average in this cohort. Because the data show time missed rather than performance after return, and the comparison group includes unknown treatment, they cannot by themselves settle whether surgery or nonoperative care gives the better result. Most in-game injuries occurred in defensive players and during contact with another player, especially tackling.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application is limited. The study does not measure performance after injury, but its position and contact-type patterns can inform where injury-prevention work is focused.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-play counselling on expected time missed. Operatively treated ruptures missed about 147 days on average, compared with about 77 days for the no-surgery or unknown group, and strains averaged 28 days. The study reports no strength, functional or performance outcomes, so it cannot show whether players return to their previous level.

records.sourceFile: Pectoralis major ruptures in the NFL - Incidence, RTP, and Performance Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Wise PM, Ptasinski AM, Gallo RA. Pectoralis major ruptures in the National Football League: incidence, RTP, and performance analysis. Orthop J Sports Med. 2021;9(6):23259671211018707.
paper.abstract: Season-ending pectoralis major ruptures in NFL players from 2010 to 2018 were identified from public reports. Most injured players were defensive, linebackers were most affected, and 54 of 63 ruptures were followed by an NFL return, with no significant change in Pro Football Focus grades among 35 players with a full season before and after injury.
paper.tldr: Pectoralis major ruptures in the NFL were concentrated in defensive players and mostly occurred in games, and most injured players returned to the league. Grades were unchanged on average in 35 players with a full season before and after injury, but the sample is small and drawn from public reports.
paper.methods: Season-ending pectoralis major ruptures in NFL players from 2010 to 2018 were identified from public injury reports, team statements and news articles. Position, age, treatment, setting, NFL Combine bench-press percentile and performance-enhancing drug suspension history were recorded. For the performance analysis, players needed at least 4 games in the season before and after their first rupture, and Pro Football Focus season grades were compared with paired t tests.
paper.findings: There were 63 ruptures in 58 players. Defensive players made up 79.3% of players (46/58; linebackers 36.2%), 76.2% of ruptures (48/63) occurred in games and 11.1% (7/63) in training, lifting or offseason activities, and 53 players had surgery while treatment was undetermined for 10 injuries. Return to NFL play was 85.7% (54/63), lowest in defensive backs (10/13). Among 35 players analysed, the mean Pro Football Focus grade was 65.10 ± 3.04 before and 65.08 ± 3.52 after injury (difference -0.02 ± 3.68; P = 0.99), with no position showing a significant change; 4 of 58 players (6.9%) had a performance-enhancing drug suspension.
paper.limitations: Injuries came from public reports, so grade, mechanism, concurrent injuries and exact treatment are unknown, some cases may have been missed, and rates could not be normalised for position or exposure. The authors' '769% increase' divides their 7.0 ruptures per year by 0.91 per year from a separate 2000 to 2010 study with different case finding, uses raw counts rather than exposure rates, and the 7.7-fold ratio would be a 669% increase. The return rate uses ruptures as the denominator (54/63) but is labelled as players, the discussion's 84.6% defensive share of ruptures does not match the counts (52/63 is 82.5%; 84.6% is the defensive return rate), and time to return could not be determined.
paper.practicalImplications: The high return rate can inform counselling for NFL players with this injury, but the small performance sample is not a guarantee of an individual's outcome. The study reports no treatment comparison, so the unchanged grades should not be read as showing that surgery restores performance. The authors link the injuries to tackling and blocking, which points prevention work toward those contact situations.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application is limited to the pre- and post-injury comparison in NFL players. Grades were unchanged on average for 35 players, which describes a group pattern rather than individual development.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-play counselling. 54 of 63 ruptures (85.7%) were followed by an NFL return, with defensive backs lowest at 10 of 13 (76.9%). The study cannot give an expected time to return and reports no strength or isokinetic outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Performance effects of functional knee brace removal and prolonged use in healthy male athlete - Lower extremity power, acceleration, speed, and agility.pdf

paper.citation: Rishiraj N, Taunton JE, Regan W, Woollard R, Lloyd-Smith R, Niven B. Performance effects of functional knee brace removal and prolonged use in healthy male athlete: Lower extremity power, acceleration, speed, and agility. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2025.
paper.abstract: Prospective crossover study of 27 healthy male athletes wearing a functional knee brace (FKB) for up to 21 hours. Vertical jump, 2 m acceleration, 10 m sprint and agility were compared after brace removal at 17.5 hours and after continued use for 21 hours. The authors report percentage improvements in most tests, but none of the comparisons reached statistical significance.
paper.tldr: Healthy male athletes showed no statistically significant change in jump, acceleration, sprint or agility after removing a functional knee brace at 17.5 hours or continuing it to 21 hours. The percentage changes are small, and the reported improvements should not be read as a performance effect.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures crossover study in 27 healthy male provincial basketball and national field hockey players. After 17.5 hours of brace use, athletes were randomly selected to remove the brace (n = 12) or continue it (n = 15), and four performance tests were compared with earlier sessions using unpaired t tests and Cohen's effect sizes.
paper.findings: Vertical jump changed by +2.7% after brace removal (P = 0.704) and +3.1% after continued use (P = 0.661). Across the four tests, changes ranged from 0.5% slower to 3.1% better, with effect sizes from trivial to small, and none of the comparisons was statistically significant. The authors describe the changes as performance improvements, although the results report no significant difference.
paper.limitations: The removal and continued-use groups were small (12 and 15) and were compared with different earlier sessions (S5 and S11), so time, fatigue and familiarization are confounded, and fatigue was not measured. By the authors' own a priori power table, groups of 10 to 20 had power below 0.80 for vertical jump and agility, so small effects could have been missed. Every comparison was non-significant, so the abstract's conclusion of improved performance overstates the findings, and results may not apply to women or athletes at risk of ACL injury.
paper.practicalImplications: In healthy male athletes, removing a functional knee brace after 17.5 hours or continuing it for 21 hours did not produce a significant change in vertical jump, acceleration, sprint or agility. Brace decisions for healthy athletes should not rest on expected performance gains or losses from these data alone. Because the study did not test injured knees, these results do not settle brace decisions after ACL injury.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study shows no significant change in jump height, 2 m acceleration, 10 m sprint or T-test agility in healthy male athletes after 17.5 to 21 hours of functional brace use. The changes were small and not significant, so the study shows neither a performance benefit nor a cost.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport, because it tested healthy athletes with intact knees rather than athletes returning from ACL reconstruction or other injury. It also does not show whether brace use changes re-injury risk.

records.sourceFile: Performance-enhancing effects of inhaled medications - Implications for heart, muscle function, and doping detection in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Cricco R, Segreti A, Stirpe E, Ferro A, Ciancio M, Cipriani F, et al. Performance-Enhancing Effects of Inhaled Medications: Implications for Heart, Muscle Function, and Doping Detection in Athletes. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2025;10:462.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of how inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids may affect the heart, skeletal muscle and performance in athletes, and how WADA thresholds and detection methods apply. The authors conclude that ergogenic effects are mainly seen at supratherapeutic doses, and that urinary thresholds remain hard to interpret.
paper.tldr: Inhaled asthma and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction medicines can affect heart rhythm and, at high doses, muscle performance. Athletes who need these medicines should stay within WADA dose limits and use the TUE process when they must exceed them.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search method; the article states that no new data were created or analysed. It draws on cited trials, WADA documents and news reports of doping cases, and summarises cardiovascular, muscle and detection evidence in tables.
paper.findings: The review reports that high or supratherapeutic inhaled doses (for example terbutaline) raised strength, sprint performance and lean mass in some trials of trained men, while standard inhaled salbutamol doses had limited or no effect on strength or sprint performance in non-asthmatic athletes. It lists tachycardia, arrhythmia, QTc prolongation and hypokalaemia as cardiovascular risks, mainly with overuse, and reports that inhaled corticosteroids have little ergogenic effect.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so its coverage cannot be checked. Many of the ergogenic and mechanistic studies it cites are small trials, and the authors describe the findings as dose-dependent and mixed. Its regulatory details cite both the 2025 and the 2026 WADA Prohibited Lists, so current dose and urine limits need checking against the official list.
paper.practicalImplications: Inhaled beta-2 agonists at standard doses are reported to have little performance effect in non-asthmatic athletes, and effects appear mainly above therapeutic use. Athletes using inhalers for asthma or EIB should keep to WADA dose limits and apply for a TUE when they need more, noting the cited finding that exercise and dehydration raised urinary salbutamol above 2000 ng/mL after 1600 micrograms inhaled. Check the current Prohibited List before advising on any inhaled medicine.
paper.athleteDev: Inhaled beta-2 agonists at supratherapeutic doses may improve sprint and strength outcomes in some trials, but standard inhaled doses show little benefit in non-asthmatic athletes. The review does not support using inhalers to improve training adaptation or performance.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport, injury or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform clearance decisions. Athletes returning from asthma or EIB treatment would need their own clinical assessment and TUE status checked.

records.sourceFile: Performance‐enhancing substances in sport - A scientometric review of 75 years of research.pdf

paper.citation: Carollo A, Corazza O, Mantovani M, Silvestrini N, Rabin O, Esposito G. Performance-enhancing substances in sport: A scientometric review of 75 years of research. Drug Test Anal. 2024.
paper.abstract: Scientometric review of doping research using Scopus records (search run March 2023) and document co-citation analysis. It maps the main countries, journals, authors and seven research clusters in performance-enhancing substance research from 1948 to 2023.
paper.tldr: Doping research has concentrated on established classes such as anabolic agents and peptide hormones, and detection methods have advanced. Research on contaminated supplements and newer substances is comparatively thin, so athlete and staff education needs to keep pace.
paper.methods: Scientometric review: a Scopus title and abstract search (English-language documents, run 9 March 2023) returned 4,330 documents, analysed with bibliometrix and CiteSpace. A PRISMA flowchart is provided, and among g-index, TOP N and TOP N% networks the TOP N (N=7) document co-citation network was chosen for its structural properties. There is no quality appraisal of the documents.
paper.findings: The collection contained 4,330 documents from 1948 to 2023, led by Drug Testing and Analysis (399 documents), with mainly German, US and UK affiliations. The co-citation network had 363 nodes, 1,092 links and seven clusters (largest: athlete biological passport, detection of peptide hormone abuse, image and performance enhancers). Of 51 documents with citation bursts, six were duplicates; the strongest bursts were Ntoumanis et al. (2014, 25.66) and Lasne and Ceaurriz (2000, 17.66), with Catlin et al. (2004) at 16.61 in Table 2.
paper.limitations: The authors note that a Scopus-only, English-only search run in 2023 may miss relevant publications and search terms. Co-citation and citation burst measure influence in the literature, not clinical or analytical quality. The text and tables disagree in places: Catlin et al. burst strength is 17.61 in the text but 16.61 in Table 2, and cluster #10 silhouette is 0.996 in the text but 0.986 in Table 1; table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: For anti-doping and athlete education planning, the review supports continued education on doping risks, with attention to contaminated supplements and emerging substances that the authors find under-studied. Use it as a map of the research landscape rather than as a ranking of substance risk.
paper.athleteDev: The performance application is indirect: the research base is strongest on anabolic agents and peptide hormones and thinner on contaminated supplements. The review does not evaluate the performance effect of any substance.
paper.rtp: This review does not address return to sport, injury or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.
